Declared emperor by the Senate at nearly 66 after Domitian's assassination, this former servant of Nero who helped expose the Pisonian conspiracy ruled Rome only from AD 96 to 98 — who was he?
Nerva: Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98. Nerva (born Marcus Cocceius Nerva; 8 November 30 – 27 January 98) was a Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98.
Fulfilling a prophecy despite his father's attempt to thwart it, which mythical king of Thebes unwittingly killed his father and married his mother?
Oedipus: Mythical Greek king of Thebes. Oedipus (UK:, also US:; Ancient Greek: Οἰδίπους Oidípous, lit. 'swollen foot') was a mythical Greek king of Thebes.
In Greek myth, this first human woman was fashioned by Hephaestus at Zeus's command and later opened a jar that unleashed evil upon the world — who was she?

Holding a doctorate in clinical psychology though he let his license lapse in 2006, this television personality got his start on The Oprah Winfrey Show before launching his own advice program in 2002 — who is he?
Phil McGraw: American television host and psychologist (born 1950)

Born at Windsor Castle with her grandmother, the queen, in attendance, this granddaughter of a British monarch married her father's cousin, a Royal Navy officer, and later became Marchioness of Milford Haven — who was she?
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine: Marchioness of Milford Haven (1863–1950)
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine
This self-described separatist was at the center of a 1992 armed standoff with federal agents in Idaho that left his wife and son dead, and he later received $3.1 million in compensation — who is he?

A top West Point graduate and U.S. Army engineer for 32 years, he switched sides to command the Army of Northern Virginia until its 1865 surrender, earning fame as one of the war's craftiest tacticians. Which Confederate general is it?
Robert E. Lee: Confederate States Army general (1807–1870)
Serving as Grand Vizier under Süleyman the Magnificent, this Ottoman statesman married the sultan's daughter Mihrimah in 1539, earning an epithet meaning 'son-in-law' — who is he?
Rüstem Pasha: Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire (1544–1553, 1555–1561)

Taking his regnal name — which meant "the legitimate king" — from an ancient ruler of Akkad, this Neo-Assyrian monarch founded a new dynastic line and aspired to conquer the known world before dying in battle in 705 BC. Who was he?
Sargon II: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Over the course of his seventeen-year reign, Sargon substantially expanded Assyrian territory and enacted important political and military reforms.
In 1902, this Indian princely ruler issued one of India's earliest affirmative-action orders, reserving half of government jobs and education for backward classes — who was he?
Shahu of Kolhapur: Indian ruler and social reformer (1894 to 1922)

In February 1979, Chinese forces launched a surprise invasion of their southern neighbor in retaliation for its overthrow of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, withdrawing after about a month — what was this clash called?
Sino-Vietnamese War: War between China and Vietnam in 1979.
This Indonesian general became his country's second president in 1967, two years after his troops put down an attempted coup — who is he?
Suharto: President of Indonesia from 1967 to 1998.
Built during Solomon's reign in the 10th century BCE and later rebuilt after the Babylonian exile, this sacred structure stood as the central place of Israelite worship in the Old City — what was it?
Temple in Jerusalem: Former places of Israelite and Jewish worship.
Born Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, this leader of Brazil's Inconfidência Mineira independence plot was hanged in 1792 and is now a national hero — by what one-word nickname is he remembered?
Tiradentes: 18th-century Brazilian revolutionary and national hero.
Explicitly authorized by the Constitution, this independent government agency replaced a Cabinet department in 1971 and holds a legal monopoly on traditional letter delivery — which agency?
United States Postal Service: Independent agency of the U.S. federal government.
Born in Leningrad and working 16 years as a KGB foreign intelligence officer, this politician has served as the de facto Russian leader since 1999 — who is he?
Vladimir Putin: President of Russia (2000–2008; since 2012)
Canada's first French-Canadian prime minister, he served 15 unbroken years from 1896 and built his legacy on compromise between English and French Canada — who is he?
Wilfrid Laurier: Prime Minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911. Sir Henri Charles Wilfrid Laurier (November 20, 1841 – February 17, 1919) was the seventh prime minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911.
A computer engineer by training, this Mexican senator and former Mexico City borough mayor ran as a coalition's nominee for the 2024 presidential election. Who is she?
An electrical engineer who was branded a "rightist" for criticizing Mao's economic policies during the Hundred Flowers Campaign, he went on to serve as China's premier from 1998 to 2003 — who is he?
Zhu Rongji: Premier of China from 1998 to 2003. Born in Changsha, Hunan, Zhu became a member of the CCP in 1949, the same year the People's Republic of China was established.
Which of these people was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Marie Curie is a physicist. Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
Which one below is best known as a chemist?
Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim is a chemist. Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim is a German chemist, science communicator, television presenter and YouTuber.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was Carl Linnaeus born?
Carl Linnaeus: Linnaeus was the son of a curate and was born in Råshult, in the countryside of Småland, southern Sweden.
In what year was Bernard Arnault born?
Bernard Arnault: Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.
In what year was Jens Stoltenberg born?
Jens Stoltenberg was born in Oslo to diplomat and politician Thorvald Stoltenberg and politician Karin Stoltenberg (née Heiberg).
In what year did Jim Lovell die?
Jim Lovell: James Arthur Lovell Jr. (LUV-əl; March 25, 1928 – August 7, 2025) was an American astronaut, naval aviator, test pilot, and mechanical engineer.
In what year did Werner Heisenberg die?
Werner Heisenberg: Heisenberg published his Umdeutung paper in 1925, a major reinterpretation of old quantum theory.
In what year was Uranium discovered?
Uranium is a chemical element; it has symbol U and atomic number 92.
In what year was Cobalt discovered?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Ciprofloxacin: Pfizer. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.
Which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 from?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Soviet Union. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Who is credited with discovering Tucana?
Tucana: Petrus Plancius. Tucana (The Toucan) is a constellation in the southern sky, named after the toucan, a South American bird.
Who is credited with discovering Cro-Magnon?
Cro-Magnon: Louis Lartet. Cro-Magnons produced Upper Palaeolithic cultures, the first major one being the Aurignacian, which was succeeded by the Gravettian by 30,000 years ago.
Who is credited with discovering Makemake?
Makemake: Michael E. Brown. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, this family of hook-billed raptors includes buzzards, vultures, and kites across 75 genera — which family is this?
Accipitridae is one of the four families within the order Accipitriformes, and is a family of small to large birds of prey with strongly hooked bills and variable morphology based on diet.
This English academic and broadcaster, an anatomist and archaeologist by training, was president of the charity Humanists UK from 2019 to 2022 — who is she?
Alice Roberts (born 19 May 1973) is an English academic, anatomist, archaeologist, TV presenter and author.

Its name means 'unlike other shrimp.' Known best from the Burgess Shale, this extinct radiodont swam with body flaps and stared out through huge compound eyes packed with lenses — what was this stem-arthropod?

Anomalocaris (from Ancient Greek, meaning "anomalous", and, meaning "shrimp", with the intended meaning "unlike other shrimp") is an extinct genus of radiodont, an order of early-diverging stem-group marine arthropods.

Caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, this infection hides in plain sight — over 85% of cases have no symptoms at all — yet in children it can stunt weight gain and trigger learning problems. What's the disease called?
Ascariasis is a disease caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. The eggs hatch in the intestines, the larvae burrow through the gut wall, and migrate to the lungs via the blood.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.
This rigid, mineralized organ of the vertebrate skeleton produces both red and white blood cells and helps regulate the body's acid-base balance — what is it?
Bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.
This soft, silvery-white metal shares group 12 of the periodic table with zinc and mercury, resembling zinc in its chemistry and mercury in its low melting point — what element, symbol Cd, is it?
Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.
This neuropsychiatric syndrome, often linked to mood or psychotic disorders, can leave a person nearly motionless for days or cause repetitive, purposeless movements. What is it?
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
Native to East Asia and blooming late in the season, these autumn flowers of the daisy family are associated in the Northern Hemisphere with the month of November. What flower is it?
Chrysanthemum (kriss-), sometimes abbreviated to mums or chrysanths, are perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that bloom in the autumn.
This highly poisonous member of the carrot family can grow to nearly 8 feet tall, with hollow, maroon-spotted stems and a famously unpleasant odor — what plant is it?
Conium maculatum (British English) or poison hemlock (in North America), is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.
This Zambian-born economist turned four of her five books into New York Times bestsellers, including a provocative argument that foreign aid actually holds Africa back — who is she?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo (born 2 February 1969) is a Zambian-born economist and author, known for her analysis of macroeconomics and global affairs.
This Canadian optical physicist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing chirped pulse amplification, a breakthrough in pulsed lasers. Who is she?
Donna Strickland (born May 27, 1959) is a Canadian optical physicist and pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers.
Psychology, medicine, history, and even computer science all study these pleasure-or-displeasure states, which still lack any agreed scientific definition — what are they?
Emotion are physical and mental states brought on by neurophysiological changes, variously associated with thoughts, feelings, behavioral responses, and a degree of pleasure or displeasure.
Known for thin, tapered wings built for high-speed flight and rapid turns, this genus of roughly 40 raptor species includes types called hobbies and kestrels — what are they?
Falcon are birds of prey in the genus Falco, which includes about 40 species.
This West Point graduate, eighth in his class of 670, commanded Apollo 8's historic flight around the Moon in 1968 — who is he?
Frank Borman (March 14, 1928 - November 7, 2023) was an American United States Air Force (USAF) colonel, aeronautical engineer, NASA astronaut, test pilot, and businessman.
The most aggressive and common cancer to originate in the brain, this tumor is thought to arise from cells called astrocytes and carries a grim prognosis — what is it?
Glioblastoma (GBM), is the most aggressive and most common type of cancer that originates in the brain, and has a very poor prognosis for survival.
Caused by a group of enteroviruses, this common infection opens with a fever and then sprinkles blistering spots on exactly the three body parts named in its label. What is it?
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses. It typically begins with a fever and feeling generally unwell.
This small rodent, with a pointed snout and a long, nearly hairless tail, has thrived by living alongside humans to the point that truly wild populations are now rare — what animal is it?
House mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length is often understood as roughly the width of a human thumb — name the unit?
Inch (symbol: in or) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.
This American psychiatrist and Communist Party USA member is best remembered today for her romantic relationship with J. Robert Oppenheimer — who was she?
Jean Tatlock (February 21, 1914 - January 4, 1944) was an American psychiatrist.
This Afghan-American author sought asylum in the U.S. as a teenager and later wrote a bestselling debut novel set in his homeland before working as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini (Pashto/; born March 4, 1965) is an Afghan and American novelist, UNHCR goodwill ambassador, and former physician.
This American computer scientist won the 2013 Turing Award for taming the chaos of distributed systems — and, on the side, created the document-preparation system LaTeX — who is he?
Leslie Lamport (born February 7, 1941) is an American computer scientist and mathematician.
This SI unit quantifies the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source, weighted by how sensitive the human eye is to different wavelengths — what is it?
Lumen (unit) (symbol: lm) is the SI unit of luminous flux, which quantifies the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source.

In 1835 she and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and decades later this Scottish polymath's name topped John Stuart Mill's women's-suffrage petition. Who is she?
Mary Somerville (ne Fairfax, formerly Greig; 1780-1872) was a Scottish scientist, writer, and polymath.
Built primarily from stainless steel, this Soviet supersonic interceptor could exceed Mach 3.2, but doing so risked wrecking its own engines. What aircraft is it?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 (NATO reporting name: Foxbat) is a supersonic interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft that is among the fastest military aircraft to enter service.
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American thinker is considered the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines. Who was he?
Norbert Wiener (November 26, 1894 - March 18, 1964) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and philosopher.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.
Built for the sea, it sports a spiny tongue and powerful jaws to grip slippery fish, then swallows them whole mid-swim. Which animal splits its life half on land, half in the water?
Penguin are a group of flightless semi-aquatic sea birds which live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere.
The sole genus in its plant subfamily, this evergreen conifer bears needle-like leaves in bunches of two to five and carries its seeds on woody cones — name the tree?
Pine is any conifer in the genus Pinus of the family Pinaceae.

Caused by the loss of function of specific genes on chromosome 15, this rare genetic disorder leads to weak muscles and poor feeding in infancy, then constant hunger and risk of obesity in childhood — what's it called?

Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare genetic disorder caused by a loss of function of specific genes on chromosome 15. A similar mechanism occurs in Angelman syndrome, except the defective chromosome 15 is from the mother, or two copies are from the father.
The sole member of the genus Setonix, this cat-sized, mainly nocturnal Australian marsupial famously inhabits Rottnest Island — what is it?
Quokka (Setonix brachyurus) is a small macropod about the size of a domestic cat.
First created near Darmstadt in 1994 and named for the physicist who discovered X-rays, this extremely radioactive element exists as only a handful of atoms with no practical use — which one is it?
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Found on every continent but Antarctica and numbering over 2,500 species, this eight-legged arachnid curves a stinger-tipped tail over its back — what is it?

Scorpion (order Scorpiones) are predatory arachnids with eight legs, a pair of grasping pincers (or Chelae) and a narrow, segmented tail, often carried in a characteristic forward curve over the back and always ending with a stinger.
This vertebrate organ system serves three main functions, protection, regulation, and sensation, and in mammals is made of multiple layers of ectodermal tissue. What is it?

Skin is the layer of usually soft, flexible outer tissue covering the body of a vertebrate animal, with three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation. The adjective cutaneous means "of the skin" (from Latin cutis 'skin').

Described as the most extreme form of malnutrition, this severe shortfall of caloric energy is so grave that deliberately inflicting it on a population is a crime under international law — what is it?
Starvation is a severe deficiency in caloric energy intake, below the level needed to maintain an organism's life.
These large, often hairy spiders of the family Theraphosidae number over a thousand species, and New World pet varieties can flick irritating 'urticating hairs' at threats. What creatures are they?
Tarantula are a group of large and often hairy spiders of the family Theraphosidae.

Proposing an information management system in March 1989 and implementing the first successful client-server exchange that November, this English computer scientist invented HTML, HTTP and the URL system — who is he?
Tim Berners-Lee (born 8 June 1955), also known as TimBL, is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web, HTML, the URL system, and HTTP.
What is the medical term for having dangerously high levels of urea in the blood, typically caused by kidney failure?

Uremia is the condition of having high levels of urea in the blood. It is the signs, symptoms and results from laboratory tests which result from inadequate excretory, regulatory, and endocrine function of the kidneys.
His 1925 Umdeutung paper reinterpreted old quantum theory, and two years later he published a famous uncertainty principle — which German physicist was he?

Werner Heisenberg (5 December 1901 - 1 February 1976) was a German theoretical physicist, one of the main pioneers of the theory of quantum mechanics and a principal scientist in the German nuclear program during World War II.
Also known as the empirical guideline, this statistical shorthand describes the percentage of values within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution — which one?
Transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly, this parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei is better known in humans as 'sleeping sickness' — what's its formal name?
African trypanosomiasis: Parasitic disease also known as sleeping sickness.

This exaggerated immune response occurs when the body mistakes a harmless substance for a threat, triggering histamine release from mast cells and conditions like hay fever or anaphylaxis. What is this reaction called?
Allergy: Immune system response to a substance that most people tolerate well.
Considered the father of the exact and natural sciences in Armenia, this 7th-century polymath wrote the first known Armenian geographic work — who was he?
This psychological state describes a lack of feeling, motivation, or concern, sitting on a spectrum between normal drive and akinetic mutism — what is it called?
Apathy: State of indifference, or the suppression of emotions.

With the symbol At and atomic number 85, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, so radioactive that a macroscopic sample would instantly vaporize itself — what element is it?
Astatine: Chemical element with atomic number 85 (At). It is the rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust, occurring only as the decay product of various heavier elements.

The most widespread bird in its family, found on every continent except Antarctica (where only stray vagrants appear), this species has blue upperparts, a deeply forked tail, and usually nests in man-made structures — what is it?
Barn swallow: Species of bird. The barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica.
This English musician played bass on the Rolling Stones' first nineteen studio albums across three decades before later fronting his own blues outfit, the Rhythm Kings — who is he?
Developed alongside the 707 airliner from the same prototype, this narrower, shorter jet became the U.S. Air Force's first jet-powered refueling tanker in 1957 — name the aircraft?
Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker: US military aerial refueling and transport aircraft.
Sold under the brand name Pulmicort, this steroid drug treats asthma when inhaled but also comes as a nasal spray for allergies and a rectal foam for bowel disease — which medication?
This highly contagious virus, spread through feces, can kill up to 91% of untreated dogs and wolves and also strikes foxes, cats, and skunks — what is it?
Canine parvovirus: Contagious virus mainly affecting dogs.
Native to Madagascar, this flowering plant known as the Madagascar periwinkle is the source of two major cancer-fighting drugs — what is it?
Catharanthus roseus: Species of flowering plant in the family Apocynaceae.
Its roasted root has long served as a coffee substitute, while today its extracted inulin shows up as a sweetener and fiber additive in packaged foods — which blue-flowered plant?
Chicory: Flowering plant in the daisy family.
Found in birds, reptiles, amphibians, and egg-laying mammals like the platypus, which single all-purpose body opening handles digestion, reproduction, and waste?
The heaviest songbird on Earth and the most widely distributed of all the corvids, this all-black passerine averages 25 inches long across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Common raven: Large, black species of passerine bird.
First described in 1963, this rare disorder from a partial deletion on chromosome 5 gets its French name from the distinctive feline-sounding cry of affected infants — what is it called?
Cri du chat syndrome: Human medical condition.

This English broadcaster is the only person to have won BAFTA Awards in black-and-white, colour, high-definition, 3D, and 4K — a span made possible by a presenting career that began with Zoo Quest in 1954. Who is this natural historian?
David Attenborough: English broadcaster and natural historian (born 1926)

A lean, wedge-skulled medium canine found in Australia and split off from the New Guinea singing dog, this animal's very classification — dog, wolf, or its own species — is still hotly debated — what is it?
Dingo: Canid species native to Australia.

Anatomically like us, some of the oldest remains of this species come from Ethiopia's Omo-Kibish site, dated to roughly 233,000 to 196,000 years ago — what term distinguishes them from archaic humans?
Early modern human: Old Stone Age ''Homo sapiens''
This inner lining of the uterus sheds during menstruation but thickens dramatically to help form the placenta during pregnancy — what is it?
Endometrium: Lining of the mammalian uterus. It has a basal layer and a functional layer: the basal layer contains stem cells which regenerate the functional layer.
This warbler's head marking gives it its name — dark in the male, chestnut in the female — and its closest relative is the garden warbler. What bird is it?
Eurasian blackcap: Bird in the Old World warbler family from Eurasia and Africa.
This German mathematician's 1872 Erlangen program reorganized all of geometry by its underlying symmetry groups, and he later turned Göttingen into a world center of research — who was he?
Home to the radius and ulna joined by the interosseous membrane, this region of the arm lies between the elbow and the wrist — what is it?
Forearm: Region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist.
Naming his most famous pistol after his 17th patent — not for holding seventeen rounds, as many assume — this Austrian engineer got his design into Austrian service in 1982 — who was he?
Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland

Making up about 15% of all brain tumors and thought to arise from cells called astrocytes, this aggressive cancer often announces itself only with vague headaches or sudden personality changes — what is it?
Glioblastoma: Aggressive type of brain cancer. Initial signs and symptoms of glioblastoma are nonspecific.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can be up to 6% caffeine — double a green coffee bean — making it a staple in Brazilian soft drinks and energy drinks — which plant?
Also known as the Burgundy snail and served as escargot, this large air-breathing land snail native to Europe has a globular brown shell — what species is it?
German anthropologist Otto Schoetensack named this archaic human species in 1908 based on a jawbone found near the village of Mauer — then Europe's oldest known human fossil. Which species?

Homo heidelbergensis: Extinct species of archaic human. H. heidelbergensis has been regarded as either the last common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans; or as a completely separate lineage.
Formed when chlorine dissolves in water, this compound is the main disinfecting agent in chlorine solutions — and your own white blood cells make it to fight off invading germs. What is it?
Hypochlorous acid: Chemical compound. Hypochlorous acid is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula ClOH, also written as HClO, HOCl, or ClHO.

This neurological emergency is sudden bleeding directly into brain tissue or its fluid-filled cavities — not from a blocked vessel, but a burst one — causing anything from headache to sudden paralysis. What is it?
Intracerebral hemorrhage: Type of intracranial bleeding that occurs within the brain tissue itself.
He won the Fields Medal in 1954 and, nearly half a century later, the very first Abel Prize in 2003 — which French mathematician of algebraic topology and geometry is it?

Conceived as a high-speed 'Schnellbomber' for the German Luftwaffe, this twin-engined WWII aircraft evolved into everything from a night fighter to the explosive lower half of composite 'Mistel' combinations — what is it?
Junkers Ju 88: German twin-engined multirole combat aircraft.

Nicknamed 'acid' and 'Lucy' and derived from the ergot fungus, this semisynthetic hallucinogen is so potent that 20 micrograms produces noticeable effects — yet no fatal human overdose has ever been documented — what is it?
Sold under the brand name Xyzal, this less-sedating second-generation antihistamine for hay fever and hives was patented in 1965 but not approved in the US until 2007 — what is it?
Levocetirizine: Antihistamine medication. It is classified as a second-generation antihistamine and works by blocking histamine H1-receptors.
Nicknamed the sea devil, frogfish, or fishing frog, this species anchors a major commercial fishery in the Irish Sea and ranges from the Barents Sea to the Mediterranean — which fish?
Lophius piscatorius: Species of fish. Lophius piscatorius, commonly known as the angler, toadfish, sea frog, fishing frog, frogfish, or sea devil, is a species of Lophius in the family Lophiidae.
This category of health conditions arises from too few, too many, or an imbalance of nutrients, and can cause anything from stunted growth to obesity. What is it called?
Malnutrition: Medical condition caused by receiving too little or too many nutrients.

Entering US Navy service in 1961 before the Marines and Air Force adopted it too, this twin-engine supersonic jet became America's most-produced supersonic military aircraft with 5,195 built — which aircraft?
McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II: Fighter aircraft family developed from 1958.
Sold as Flagyl, this antibiotic and antiprotozoal fights everything from giardiasis to trichomoniasis — but it's notorious for leaving a metallic taste in your mouth — what is it?
Metronidazole: Antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
With velvety fur, tiny eyes, and powerful digging forelimbs, this subterranean mammal aerates garden soil and feasts on earthworms and slugs despite being seen as a pest — what is it?
Mole (animal): Common name for several small mammals.
This condition describes an abnormally dilated pupil that remains enlarged even in bright light, often triggered by trauma, disease, or certain drugs — what is it called?
Mydriasis: Excessive dilation of the pupil.
This 17th-century Dane was a pioneer of both anatomy and geology — he doubted that fossils "grew" in the ground — before becoming a Catholic bishop and being beatified by the Church. Who was he?
Nicolas Steno: Danish scientist and Catholic bishop (1638 – 1686)
Known as holy basil and sacred within the Vaishnava tradition of Hinduism, which aromatic herb is widely used in Ayurvedic tea?
Ocimum tenuiflorum: Species of flowering plant.

Most members of this order of over 200 species are solitary night hunters with broad heads, binocular vision, and feathers tuned for silent flight — though oddballs like the burrowing kind break the mold. What are they?
Owl: Birds from the order Strigiformes.
This economist and longtime New York Times columnist was the sole winner of the 2008 Nobel for his work on new trade theory and economic geography. Who is he?
First extracted from coal tar and now made from petroleum, this mildly acidic compound is a key precursor to Bakelite and nylon — what is it?
Widely planted along London's streets as a hybrid variety, this tree genus includes the sycamores of North America and can tower up to 50 meters — which genus?
Platanus: Genus of flowering plants constituting the family Platanaceae.
What is this — “Medical condition where an erection lasts excessively long”?
Priapism: Medical condition where an erection lasts excessively long. Priapism is a condition in which a penis remains erect for hours in the absence of stimulation or after stimulation has ended.
Usually caused by E. coli spreading up the urinary tract, this kidney infection typically brings fever and flank tenderness, and can be prevented by urinating after sex — what condition is it?
Pyelonephritis: Inflammation of the kidney. It is typically due to a bacterial infection, most commonly Escherichia coli.
From a startled jump to a cat automatically reorienting itself mid-fall, this involuntary, split-second reaction runs through the nervous system without needing conscious thought — what's it called?
Reflex: Automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus.
Usually hidden underground, this plant organ anchors it in place while drawing in water and nutrients — what is it?
Root: Basal organ of a vascular plant.
